pages.text:
At 6:47, a dinosaur climbed onto my chest and screamed.

"RAAAAWR," said Gus, with his whole face an inch from mine.

I didn't yell or push him off. Instead, I sat up and blinked because the room felt completely wrong. The posters were gone, the beanbag was gone, and only the bed remained alongside the box marked MISC. The wall showed pale rectangles where my life used to be.

I looked at the clock on my nightstand. It said 6:47. Saturday.

My stomach dropped all the way to the pillow.

"Gus," I said, my voice sounding like it was coming from a different room. "We're both awake. That's the only thing that's going right."

He sat back on my ribs, pleased, and the spikes on his tail knocked over the water glass on my floor. Nobody had packed that water glass. It was the last thing in my room that nobody had packed.

I realized I had slept through Sunday. I had slept through the truck. I was going to be late for school in Arizona.

Gus roared again.

I looked at the clock. 6:47.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy with messy hair, sits up in a bare bed looking terrified while Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, sits on his chest with his mouth wide open, roaring; morning light, cardboard boxes in the corner.

pages.text:
At 7:13, Waffles stole my left slipper.

He trotted past my door with the slipper hanging out of his mouth like a cigar, gave me a look that said *come and get me*, and vanished under the dining room table. I could see all the way to the back of the house from the hall because there was nothing left to block the view.

I crawled after him. Under the table were: one lost sock, one red Lego brick, and a french fry so old it had turned into a fossil. Waffles lay in the middle of them, chewing my slipper with the expression of a dog who has never had a single regret.

I stood up slowly because my legs felt like they were made of old cardboard.

"Nope," I said out loud.

Mom appeared in the doorway holding her clipboard. She had six pages stapled together and a pencil behind her ear. She looked at me, then at the dog, then at me again.

"Max, who are you talking to?"

"I'm talking to the slipper," I said. "He's stealing it."

Mom checked her list. She ticked something off without looking up.
pages.image: Max on hands and knees peers under a dining table where Waffles, a chubby corgi, chews a slipper next to a lost sock, a red Lego, and a fossilized french fry; behind Max, Gus in a green T. rex costume sits on the floor looking small.

pages.text:
At 7:22, the smoke alarm shrieked.

Dad stood on his chair in his fish apron, fanning the ceiling with a dish towel while shouting over the beeping.

"Max! Good morning! Did you know I'm reading a book about anti-gravity?"

"No," I said.

"It's impossible to put down!"

A cold spike hit my chest, and I knew what came next. I knew it in my bones, which felt like they had turned to ice.

"It's not burnt, Mira," I said before Dad could finish his sentence. "It's dark."

Dad froze. He lowered the towel, and his mustache went flat. He looked at me with real alarm, the kind of look a teacher gives when a student answers a question they haven't asked yet.

"How did you know that?" he asked.

I didn't wait for an answer. I ran to the bathroom and locked the door. My hands were shaking, so I pressed them against the cool tile of the sink.

It wasn't a dream. It wasn't a memory. It was a recording.
pages.image: Dad, a big round man with a dark mustache in a fish apron, stands on a chair fanning a screaming smoke alarm with a dish towel, looking shocked; Max in a red hoodie stands stone-faced in the doorway.

pages.text:
At 8:05, the doorbell rang, and I was already standing in the hallway with my hand on the knob.

I opened the door before the second ring had a chance to happen. Mrs. Abernathy stood there in her floral gardening hat, holding her tuna noodle casserole with the same grip she used for things she was very proud of.

"It's a hot dish," I said, looking her straight in the eye. "So be careful, you'll want a trivet."

She blinked, then looked at the dish, then back at me. Her trivet slipped from her fingers and clattered loudly on the porch steps.

"Max," Mom said from the kitchen, her voice tight and worried. "Don't tease the neighbors."

I walked back to the kitchen counter and looked down at my hand. The margin of my palm was blank, but my brain was full of lists. I grabbed a pencil from the drying rack and started writing on the back of a moving box.

*Things That Are Exactly The Same.*

1. The slipper.
2. The toast.
3. The trivet.

I looked up through the gap in the doorway. Mrs. Abernathy was bending down to pick up her trivet, and her hands were shaking, which made me feel like I had broken something that couldn't be fixed.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, stands in the doorway writing on his palm with a pencil; Mrs. Abernathy, an 80s woman in a floral hat, stands on the porch looking shocked with a casserole dish in her hands.

pages.text:
I ran.

I went out the back door and down Larkspur Lane in my slippers, my lungs burning with every breath while my feet slapped the pavement in a frantic, wet rhythm. I kept moving until the streetlights flickered and the houses blurred into a long, grey line, and then I stopped at Weller Creek.

I lay down on the bank, feeling the cool mud seep through my hoodie, and watched the brown water spin in slow, lazy circles. I closed my eyes and waited for the day to end on its own terms.

I fell asleep on purpose.

I woke up on my air mattress, the house silent except for the steady tick of the clock, and I knew exactly where I was before I even opened my eyes.

I looked up. 6:47.

A dinosaur climbed onto my chest and screamed.

"RAAAAWR."

I didn't sit up. I just lay there, staring at the ceiling, feeling the heavy weight of the T. rex hood against my ribs. That was when I understood I hadn't dreamed anything. The day wasn't a memory that I could shake off like a bad dream in class. It was a loop, a stuck video game level that refused to load the next stage. And I was the only one who knew the words.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy with messy hair, lies flat in a bare bed looking doomed while Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, sits on his chest with his mouth wide open, roaring; morning light, cardboard boxes in the corner.
